Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they’re earned or owed, not when cash actually moves. If you deliver a product in June but the customer pays in July, you record the sale in June. If you receive a bill in June but pay it in July, you record the expense in June. That matching of revenue and related costs shows how the business really performed in each period.

Cash-basis accounting records income and expenses only when money is received or paid. It’s simpler and shows actual cash flow, but results can swing based on payment timing (a big payment one month can make that month look much stronger).

Which to pick depends on complexity and reporting needs: accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing performance; cash is easier and may suit very small operations. Note: I did not use web sources for this short overview, so no external citations were added.
